body_html:
I like radial progress indicators. They save a lot of space and can communicate really complex scenarios very well.

A client recently asked me to create a radial progress indicator with multiple values, like this:

These are the times of SVG, and with SVG’s <circle>-element, it’s pretty easy:

<circle r="90" cx="100" cy="100"></circle>

To create the progress, however, is a bit more tricky UNLESS you use the wonderful “stroke-dasharray”-hack!

It’s basically a dashed line to stroke the circle with — but we’ll make one single dash the length we need, and the distance to the next dash the circumference of the circle, so we won’t ever see it. Pretty clever.

In order to create the radial progress indicator shown in the image above, we need more “layers” of dashes:

SVG markup

<div class="radial-progress-wrapper" id="radial1" itemscope itemtype="http://schema.org/ActionStatusType">
  <svg class="radial-progress" version="1.1" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">
    <circle r="90" cx="100" cy="100"></circle>
    <circle r="90" cx="100" cy="100" class="radial-progress-1" style="stroke-dasharray: 565.487px; stroke-dashoffset: 166.105px;"></circle>
    <circle r="90" cx="100" cy="100" class="radial-progress-2" style="stroke-dasharray: 565.487px; stroke-dashoffset: 194.379px;"></circle>
    <circle r="90" cx="100" cy="100" class="radial-progress-3" style="stroke-dasharray: 565.487px; stroke-dashoffset: 364.025px;"></circle>
  </svg>
  <div class="radial-progress-inner">
    <meta itemprop="name" content="Progress" />
    <h1 class="radial-progress-header" itemprop="description"><span class="radial-progress-percent">73.63</span>%</h1>
  </div>
</div>

— the CSS will be rendered from this mixin:

Mixin

@mixin radial-progress($size, $strokewidth, $color-bg, $strokes...) {
    width: $size;
    height: $size;
    @include prefixed(transform, rotate(270deg));
    stroke: $color-bg;
    stroke-width: $strokewidth;
	
	& > circle { 
		fill: transparent;
	}
	
	@each $stroke in $strokes {
    $i: index($strokes, $stroke);
	    &-#{$i} { 
			stroke: $stroke;
	    }
	}

	&-inner {
		@include prefixed(transform, translate(-50%, -50%));
		position: absolute;
		left: 50%;
		top: 50%;
	}
	&-wrapper {
		display: inline-block;
		position: relative;
	}
}

Now, let’s create a class using the mixin, with size, stroke and an array of colors:

.radial-progress {
	@include radial-progress(200px, 1rem, #dedede, lighten(#ad87c4, 10), #ad87c4, #826296, #501a71 );
}

The result can be seen in the follwing pen:

Now, to be fair, a little JavaScript is needed to actually calculate the lengths of the dashes, but let’s wait with that, because wouldn’t it be nice if the progress was animated:

For the animation, I use requestAnimationFrame, calculate the different lengths using a series of calculations, invilving:

(nRadius * Math.PI) * 2 // Circumference
nRadius - ((nRadius / 100) * value)
etc.

The complete function looks like this:

*	radial.js
*	Animated Radial Progress-indicator
*	(c)	Copyright 2015 Mads Stoumann
*/
function radial(aCircles, oTextCounter) {
	var
	aSum = [],
	i,
	nCurVal,
	nLen = aCircles.length,
	nRadius = (90 * Math.PI) * 2,
	nStep,
	nVal = 0;
	
	for (i = 0; i < nLen; i++) {
		aCircles[i].style.strokeDashoffset = nRadius;
		aCircles[i].style.strokeDasharray = nRadius;
		nVal += aCircles[i].getAttribute("data-val")-0;
		aSum.push(nRadius - ((nRadius / 100) * nVal));
	}
	
	aSum.reverse();
	nStep = ((nRadius - ((nRadius / 100) * nVal)) / (100-nVal));
	
	function _animate() {
		nCurVal = oTextCounter.innerHTML-0;
		if (nCurVal < nVal) {
			nCurVal++;
			for (i = nLen; i--;) {
				if (aSum[i] <= (nRadius - (nCurVal * nStep) + nStep)) {
					aCircles[i].style.strokeDashoffset = nRadius - (nCurVal * nStep); 
				}
			}
			oTextCounter.innerHTML = nCurVal;
			window.requestAnimationFrame(_animate);
		} 
	}
	window.requestAnimationFrame(_animate);
}
